WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000159.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000159.question: What is mercury?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000159.answer_short: Mercury (Hg) is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature — a dense, silvery 'quicksilver' found in the bright-red ore cinnabar.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000160.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000160.question: How does mercury poison the body?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000160.answer_short: Mercury is an accumulative poison that binds to enzymes and cripples them; its vapor is far more dangerous than the liquid metal.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000161.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000161.question: What does mercury have to do with the quest for immortality?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000161.answer_short: Ancient Chinese alchemists drank mercury as an immortality elixir — China's first emperor poisoned himself to death that way.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000162.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000162.question: Where does mercury exposure come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000162.answer_short: Industry, mining, farming, vaccines and dental amalgam fillings concentrate mercury in the environment — even in people whose only exposure is their fillings.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000163.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000163.question: Is the mercury in fish dangerous?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000163.answer_short: Fish carry mercury as persistent methylmercury; heavy fish-eaters hold far more, and unlike inorganic mercury it crosses the placenta into the fetus.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000164.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000164.question: What protects against mercury poisoning?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000164.answer_short: Selenium is mercury's natural antidote: the two are mutually antagonistic, and selenium shields the kidneys and fetus from mercury.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000165.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000165.question: Can dental mercury fillings affect gut bacteria?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000165.answer_short: In monkeys, vapor from dental amalgam raised antibiotic-resistant gut bacteria from 9% to 70% — dropping back to 12% once the fillings were removed.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000166.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000166.question: Why do we say 'mad as a hatter'?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000166.answer_short: The phrase comes from real poisoning: Victorian hatmakers who brushed mercury paste onto felt inhaled the vapor and went 'mad as a hatter.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000167.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000167.question: Is dental mercury linked to MS, ALS or Parkinson's?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000167.answer_short: Wallach reports dentists and patients develop high rates of MS, ALS and Parkinson's tied to mercury vapor — he cites Annette Funicello's MS.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000168.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000168.question: What are the signs of mercury poisoning?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000168.answer_short: Mostly neurological: tremors, vertigo, irritability, mood changes, salivation, mouth inflammation and diarrhea — organic mercury is the most toxic.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000169.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000169.question: What was the Minamata disaster?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000169.answer_short: In 1962 a Japanese factory dumped mercury into Minamata Bay; contaminated fish caused an epidemic of birth defects, cerebral palsy and infant death.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000170.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000170.question: What happened in the Iraq mercury poisoning?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000170.answer_short: Iraqis ate bread from seed grain treated with mercury fungicide — thousands of babies were born with brain defects, cerebral palsy and neural-tube defects.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000171.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000171.question: Do vaccines cause autism?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000171.answer_short: Wallach gives both sides — the mercury-preservative (thimerosal) hypothesis and his doubt that no other country saw the same autism surge — and leaves it open.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000062.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000062.question: How much calcium are humans designed to eat?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000062.answer_short: Wallach argues we're built for Stone-Age intakes of 1,600–3,000 mg a day; modern Americans get a fraction — as little as 300 mg.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000065.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000065.question: How much calcium is in your body, and where?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000065.answer_short: Calcium is the body's most abundant mineral (~1–1.2 kg); 99% sits in the bones and teeth, and the last 1% works in blood and cells.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000066.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000066.question: How is calcium stored in your bones?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000066.answer_short: As hydroxyapatite crystals on a protein 'bone matrix' — soak a bone in vinegar two weeks and the calcium leaches out, leaving the bendy scaffold.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000067.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000067.question: What does calcium do besides build bone?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000067.answer_short: It's a working cofactor: it releases ATP energy for muscle, drives blood clotting, moves signals across membranes, fires nerves and paces the heartbeat.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000069.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000069.question: How does the body keep blood calcium steady?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000069.answer_short: Two hormones — parathormone and calcitonin — hold serum calcium at 8.5–10.5 mg/dL, mostly by borrowing it from and returning it to bone.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000070.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000070.question: What in the modern diet drains your calcium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000070.answer_short: Fiber, salt and soft-drink phosphate force calcium out of the body — the modern diet's calcium-to-phosphorus ratio simply can't be met by eating alone.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000074.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000074.question: How many diseases does Wallach tie to calcium deficiency?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000074.answer_short: 147 — Wallach links no fewer than 147 diseases to calcium deficiency or imbalance, and says U.S. diets are so deficient that only supplements fix it.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000075.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000075.question: Which famous people did Wallach say had calcium deficiency?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000075.answer_short: He points to Pope John Paul II, Elizabeth Taylor, 'Bo' Jackson and vegan NBA star Bill Walton — all, he says, with osteoporosis or fractures.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000006.subject: cholesterol
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000006.question: Is cholesterol bad for you?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000006.answer_short: No — Wallach calls cholesterol an essential nutrient: it builds every cell membrane, all the steroid hormones, and the brain's myelin.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000054.subject: cholesterol
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000054.question: What does cholesterol actually do in the body?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000054.answer_short: It's the raw material for vitamin D, bile acids, and the adrenal stress and sex hormones — so a cholesterol deficiency can worsen menopause and flatten libido.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000003.subject: diabetes
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000003.question: What actually causes type 2 diabetes?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000003.answer_short: Wallach's stance: type 2 diabetes isn't genetic — it's a chromium and vanadium deficiency, and correcting it prevents and even reverses the disease.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000089.subject: diabetes
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000089.question: How does chromium deficiency lead to diabetes?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000089.answer_short: Chromium runs the body's blood-sugar handling; deficiency wrecks glucose tolerance (77% of 'normal' over-70s) — and Wallach cites the USDA that 90% of Americans are chromium-deficient.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000034.subject: diabetes
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000034.question: How does vanadium help with diabetes?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000034.answer_short: Vanadium mimics insulin — it makes the cell's insulin receptors more sensitive, helping the body handle glucose and carbohydrates.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000048.subject: diabetes
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000048.question: How does Wallach treat diabetes?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000048.answer_short: Start with chromium and vanadium at 250 mcg a day in the early stages — carefully, to avoid dropping blood sugar too fast ('insulin shock').

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000008.subject: diabetes
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000008.question: How did Wallach first connect diabetes to a mineral deficiency?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000008.answer_short: From the autopsy table: he saw zoo marmosets, alligators and shrews die of diabetes caused by chromium and vanadium deficiency.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000080.subject: diabetes
WAL-CLM-LETS-000080.question: Can a normal blood test miss diabetes?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000080.answer_short: Yes — a single fasting blood-sugar reading misses most diabetes and hypoglycemia; Wallach says only a six-hour glucose tolerance test reveals them.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000024.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000024.question: What is a colloidal mineral?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000024.answer_short: A mineral existing as ultra-fine particles (1–100 nanometers — 'nano-technology') suspended in liquid, too small to dissolve into single atoms the way salt does.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000060.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000060.question: Why do different mineral forms absorb so differently?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000060.answer_short: Metallic minerals are only 8–12% absorbable (3–5% after 40), chelated better, and plant-derived colloidal the most usable — which is why Wallach calls it the most critical of the 90 nutrients.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000023.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000023.question: What are chelated minerals, and do they absorb better?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000023.answer_short: Chelated minerals wrap an amino acid around each mineral, absorbing ~40–65% — a 400% jump over metallic (8–12%); on a label they read as 'picolinate' or 'amino acid chelate.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000025.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000025.question: Why can't you just swallow ground-up rock minerals?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000025.answer_short: Inorganic mineral particles are too large to cross the gut wall; only when amino acids convert them into absorbable 'crystalloids' can the intestine take them up.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000026.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000026.question: Which form of colloidal mineral is best?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000026.answer_short: The plant-derived, living organic colloid — coated in a water-loving protein, up to 98% bioavailable — is the form Wallach favors over bare 'rock flour' or industrial versions.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000099.subject: color_therapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000099.question: What is color therapy?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000099.answer_short: Using colored lights or panels for a healing effect — recorded in ancient Egypt and used in Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine; Wallach frames it as a form of light therapy.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000100.subject: color_therapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000100.question: What does each color treat in color therapy?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000100.answer_short: Wallach's color map: blue for blood pressure, fever, cuts and burns; red for low blood pressure; orange for stones; yellow for diabetes; green for ulcers, colds and breast cancer.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000101.subject: color_therapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000101.question: How is color therapy actually done?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000101.answer_short: Six techniques — the Kilner diagnostic screen, reading tissue colors, sun-charged salt bags, colored foods, 'rainbow' sun-charged water, and meditative color breathing.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000002.subject: wallach
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000002.question: What makes Dr. Wallach's approach different?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000002.answer_short: 20,000+ autopsies across 454 animal species plus 3,000 humans — a comparative-pathology record that led him to conclude 'natural causes' deaths were really nutritional deficiencies.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000020.subject: wallach
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000020.question: What are Dr. Wallach's credentials?
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000020.answer_short: A 1991 Nobel Prize nomination for linking selenium to cystic fibrosis, two research medals, co-author of the DSHEA supplement law, and credit as an early founder of epigenetics.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000005.subject: wallach
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000005.question: How did Wallach beat the FDA over omega-3?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000005.answer_short: After a long legal fight, on Sept 8, 2004 the FDA let his petition stand — allowing the claim that omega-3s cut heart-disease risk, which had been illegal to state for 65 years.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000010.subject: wallach
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000010.question: Does Wallach agree with Linus Pauling?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000010.answer_short: Not on minerals — he corrects even the two-time Nobel laureate, who dismissed minerals as secondary and capped selenium at 15 mcg (today's safe limit is 200–1,000 mcg).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000125.subject: iron
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000125.question: What is iron, and where does it come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000125.answer_short: Iron is the 4th most abundant element in Earth's crust — its ores opened the Iron Age (~1100 B.C.), and Earth's molten core is thought to be magnetized iron.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000127.subject: iron
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000127.question: Why is carbon monoxide so deadly?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000127.answer_short: Carbon monoxide binds the iron in hemoglobin ~200x more tightly than oxygen — crowding oxygen out of the blood, which is what makes it poisonous.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000128.subject: iron
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000128.question: How much iron is in your body, and where?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000128.answer_short: A healthy adult carries 3-5 g of iron; ~60-70% is 'functional' (in hemoglobin, muscle and enzymes) and 30-40% is stored in marrow and liver.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000130.subject: iron
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000130.question: What causes iron deficiency?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000130.answer_short: Wallach's list: unsupplemented pregnancy, heavy periods, chronic infection or bleeding, low stomach acid, diarrhea, and poor absorption from high-fiber diets.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000132.subject: iron
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000132.question: What helps or blocks iron absorption?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000132.answer_short: Stomach acid and vitamin C boost iron absorption; fiber and phytates block it — so Wallach says the 18 mg RDA is too low for vegans and high-fiber diets.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000173.subject: iodine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000173.question: Where is iodine found in nature?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000173.answer_short: Thinly spread through rock, water and soil — large areas of crust are iodine-free (it binds to humus), while seaweeds concentrate it up to 1,500 ppm.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000174.subject: iodine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000174.question: What is iodine, and how was it discovered?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000174.answer_short: A violet-black solid that sublimes to a violet gas — the heaviest halogen. Courtois found it in 1811 in kelp; its name is Greek 'iodes,' violet-colored.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000175.subject: iodine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000175.question: Where does commercial iodine come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000175.answer_short: Extracted from sodium iodate in Chilean saltpeter, from burnt-seaweed ash historically, and from underground brine wells in Arkansas and Oklahoma.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000176.subject: iodine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000176.question: What is iodine used for?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000176.answer_short: A classic wound antiseptic (iodine tincture) and water purifier; in medicine, radioactive iodine-131 treats thyroid cancer and an overactive thyroid.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000178.subject: iodine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000178.question: How much iodine do we take in - and how much is safe?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000178.answer_short: Americans average 170-250 mcg a day and can sweat out up to 146 mcg; metallic iodine isn't toxic even at 2,000 mcg/day long-term - a wide safety margin.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000181.subject: iodine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000181.question: What does iodine do through the thyroid?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000181.answer_short: Iodine builds thyroid hormones, which regulate digestion, heart rate, metabolism, temperature and weight - so ~1 million Americans have thyroid trouble.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000138.subject: germanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000138.question: What is germanium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000138.answer_short: A metalloid 'semiconductor' element predicted by Mendeleyev in 1871 and isolated in 1886 - 'doped' with a trace of arsenic or gallium, it makes transistors.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000141.subject: germanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000141.question: How does germanium behave in the body?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000141.answer_short: It accepts and passes electrons like a semiconductor; biologically Wallach calls it an 'electrical impulse initiator' in cells and a cofactor for oxygen use.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000142.subject: germanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000142.question: How was germanium's healing reputation discovered?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000142.answer_short: In 1950 the Japanese chemist Dr. Kazuhiko Asai found germanium in fossilized plants, and Russian researchers soon attributed anti-cancer activity to it.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000143.subject: germanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000143.question: How does germanium support the immune system?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000143.answer_short: Asai tied germanium-rich herbs to healing; germanium boosts natural killer cells, interferon-gamma, macrophages and T-suppressor cells.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000144.subject: germanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000144.question: What is Ge-132, the germanium supplement?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000144.answer_short: An organic, chelated germanium (carboxyethyl germanium sesquioxide) Asai made in 1967 - absorbed at ~30% and fully excreted within a week.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000146.subject: germanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000146.question: Why are the 'Holy Waters' of Lourdes said to heal?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000146.answer_short: Wallach's mineral explanation: the famous healing waters of Lourdes, France contain large amounts of germanium and lithium.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000148.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000148.question: Who discovered hydrogen?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000148.answer_short: Henry Cavendish (1731-1810), who made the gas in 1766 - a brilliant, painfully shy recluse who never spoke to women and gave servants orders by written note.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000149.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000149.question: What does hydrogen have to do with the Hindenburg?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000149.answer_short: Hydrogen's lightness made it the early lift gas for blimps - until a spark ignited the hydrogen-filled Hindenburg in 1937 and the industry switched to helium.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000150.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000150.question: How does hydrogen set the body's acid-base balance?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000150.answer_short: Regulating acid-base balance is really regulating hydrogen-ion (H+) levels - healthy blood is held in a narrow pH band of 7.36-7.44 by homeostatic mechanisms.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000152.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000152.question: How does the body get rid of acid?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000152.answer_short: The kidneys excrete metabolic hydrogen ions ~60% as ammonium and 40% as weak acids; the trace of free H+ left is what sets the urine's pH.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000154.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000154.question: Where is hydrogen found in the body?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000154.answer_short: Beyond water (70% of the body), hydrogen is a major part of nearly every biological molecule - carbohydrates, fats, proteins, enzymes, and DNA and RNA.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000187.subject: potassium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000187.question: Where is potassium found in nature?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000187.answer_short: A positively charged mineral in all soils (highest in alkaline ones); marine plants concentrate it most (52,000 ppm), and in animals it fills the soft tissue.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000188.subject: potassium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000188.question: What is potassium, chemically?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000188.answer_short: A silver-white alkali metal so soft you can cut it with a knife - so reactive it's never found pure in nature; Davy first isolated it by electrolysis in 1807.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000189.subject: potassium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000189.question: Is your body slightly radioactive from potassium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000189.answer_short: A little: 0.012% of natural potassium is radioactive potassium-40, so the ~140 g in your body is a lifelong part of your background radiation.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000190.subject: potassium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000190.question: Where does the name 'potassium' come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000190.answer_short: From 'potash' - the potassium-rich ash left when wood and plants are burned in pots; plants were humans' early mineral source, and it's still the main fertilizer.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000191.subject: potassium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000191.question: What is saltpeter?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000191.answer_short: Potassium nitrate (KNO3) - 'saltpeter,' looks and tastes like salt, used for centuries as a preservative and fertilizer, and one of gunpowder's three ingredients.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000116.subject: fluoride
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000116.question: What is fluorine?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000116.answer_short: The smallest, lightest and most reactive halogen ('salt former') - a pale-yellow gas so reactive it never occurs free, locked instead in minerals like fluorite.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000117.subject: fluoride
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000117.question: Who discovered fluorine, and what does its name mean?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000117.answer_short: Henri Moissan won the 1906 Nobel Prize for first isolating pure fluorine (1886), after 75 years of effort; the name is Latin 'fluere,' to flow.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000118.subject: fluoride
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000118.question: Is fluoride an essential nutrient?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000118.answer_short: Wallach says yes in trace amounts - before 1972 it was only 'considered' essential for tooth enamel, then Schwarz proved it essential for animals and humans.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000120.subject: fluoride
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000120.question: How much fluoride is in and around us?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000120.answer_short: An adult skeleton can bank up to 2.6 g of fluoride, and the average American takes in ~4.4 mg a day from food, water, toothpaste and supplements combined.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000122.subject: fluoride
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000122.question: How widespread is water fluoridation?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000122.answer_short: About 10,000 U.S. towns fluoridate water at 1 mg/L for 100 million people, reportedly cutting cavities 60-70% - but naturally high levels mottle children's teeth.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000124.subject: fluoride
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000124.question: Is fluoridated water safe?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000124.answer_short: Wallach calls it 'still highly controversial' - laying out both the cavity benefit and the fluorosis, bone-fracture and cancer concerns without a flat verdict.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000097.subject: copper
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000097.question: What is copper, and where does its name come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000097.answer_short: A soft reddish metal - only 0.007% of Earth's crust. Its name is Latin 'cuprum' ('from Cyprus,' where Rome mined it), and it was one of humanity's first metals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000106.subject: copper
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000106.question: What are normal copper levels in the blood?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000106.answer_short: Average plasma copper is about 87-153 (women) and 89-137 (men) micrograms per deciliter, and ~90% of it rides on a carrier protein called ceruloplasmin.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000111.subject: copper
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000111.question: What raises blood copper, and what is copper overload?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000111.answer_short: Copper roughly doubles in pregnancy and on the pill, and rises with infection, liver disease and pellagra; overload shows as copper Kayser-Fleischer rings in the eye.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000091.subject: chromium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000091.question: Why is chromium so easy to lose and hard to absorb?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000091.answer_short: Sugar flushes chromium out in urine (up 300% for 12 hrs) and food chromium is barely retained; form decides - ~25% of chelated vs up to 98% of colloidal is absorbed.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000092.subject: chromium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000092.question: Has Americans' chromium level been falling?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000092.answer_short: Yes - the young hold more chromium than the old, unsupplemented tissue steadily drops with age, and Wallach charts a steep fall in average American blood chromium since 1948.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000093.subject: chromium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000093.question: How was chromium discovered, and why does it color gemstones?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000093.answer_short: Found in 1797 by Vauquelin and named from Greek 'chroma' (color) for its vivid compounds - trace chromium makes rubies red, emeralds green, and alexandrite shift color.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000040.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000040.question: Does gold treat arthritis?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000040.answer_short: Wallach is cautious - doctors add gold to aspirin for arthritis, but he stresses it only helps ACTIVE joint inflammation, not advanced, destructive rheumatoid arthritis.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000041.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000041.question: Is gold used to treat cancer?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000041.answer_short: One form is: gold-198, a short-lived radioactive isotope (2.7-day half-life), is used as radiation therapy for some cancers - a medical use Wallach notes, not nutrition.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000033.subject: aluminum
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000033.question: Is aluminum in our food, and is that dangerous?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000033.answer_short: Unavoidable but normal, Wallach says: aluminum is Earth's most abundant metal (~12% of crust) and every plant takes it up - so no food or natural water is free of it.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000034.subject: aluminum
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000034.question: Does aluminum cause Alzheimer's disease?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000034.answer_short: Wallach says no - he calls it a myth from 'a single faulty study,' citing later work (Oxford 1992, a 2007 German assessment) that found no proven dietary-aluminum link.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000195.subject: krypton
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000195.question: What is krypton - the Superman element?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000195.answer_short: Despite Superman's 'kryptonite,' real krypton is a harmless, unreactive noble gas - which Wallach says 'may in fact be an essential element for all vertebrates.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000196.subject: krypton
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000196.question: How was krypton discovered?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000196.answer_short: Noble gases had no place in Mendeleyev's 1869 table; after argon forced a new column, Sir William Ramsay isolated krypton in 1898, naming it from Greek 'kryptos,' hidden.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000197.subject: krypton
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000197.question: Can krypton form compounds - didn't Pauling predict it?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000197.answer_short: Yes - though noble gases were thought inert, Linus Pauling used quantum mechanics in 1933 to predict krypton fluoride; Neil Bartlett proved him right by making KrF2 in 1966.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000134.subject: gallium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000134.question: What is gallium - the metal that melts in your hand?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000134.answer_short: A soft, aluminum-like metal so low-melting it liquefies from your body heat, yet has the widest liquid range of any metal; named for Gallia (the Latin name for France).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000136.subject: gallium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000136.question: Is gallium used in cancer medicine?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000136.answer_short: Yes - gallium-67 (78-hour half-life), one of medicine's first man-made isotopes, gathers in cancers like melanoma, letting it treat them with little harm to nearby tissue.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000018.subject: essential_nutrients
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000018.question: Why do the 90 essential nutrients matter?
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000018.answer_short: They're the cofactors enzymes need to work - miss one and the enzyme stalls. Most people never reach optimal levels, a 'subclinical' shortfall felt as fatigue and low mood.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000019.subject: essential_nutrients
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000019.question: Can you get all your nutrition from food alone?
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000019.answer_short: Wallach says no - food itself is depleted (vitamins down 37%, trace minerals 77%), so he calls a full 90-nutrient supplement program a cornerstone of health.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000013.subject: essential_nutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000013.question: How depleted is the food supply?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000013.answer_short: A USDA comparison (1975-2004) shows steep losses - broccoli lost 54% of its calcium, apples 60% of their iron - so Wallach says food alone can't supply enough minerals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000014.subject: essential_nutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000014.question: What are the 90 essential nutrients?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000014.answer_short: Of 79+ elements found in the body, Wallach counts 60 minerals as essential - plus 16 vitamins, 12 amino acids and 3 essential fatty acids: the '90 essentials.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000017.subject: essential_nutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000017.question: How does a mineral deficiency progress before you notice?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000017.answer_short: In four hidden stages: initial (just 'low energy,' tests normal), compensated (cravings, odd symptoms), decompensated (real disease), then clinical (full disease, even death).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000059.subject: vitamins
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000059.question: What are vitamins?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000059.answer_short: Organic compounds the body needs in tiny daily amounts but can't make itself; they work mostly as coenzymes (switching enzymes on) and supply no calories and no body mass.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000060.subject: vitamins
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000060.question: What are the different kinds of vitamins?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000060.answer_short: Three classes: fat-soluble (A, D, E, K - need fat/bile to absorb), water-soluble (the B's and C, cell-energy cofactors), and flavanols (the dark-chocolate bioflavonoids).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000007.subject: vitamins
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000007.question: What happens if you're vitamin-deficient during pregnancy?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000007.answer_short: Wallach warns it can cause catastrophic birth defects - among them neural-tube defects, cleft lip and palate, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis and heart defects.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000009.subject: vitamins
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000009.question: Does the birth-control pill deplete a vitamin?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000009.answer_short: Yes - Wallach says 15-20% of women on the pill show vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency: malaise, depression, and glucose intolerance (trouble handling blood sugar).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000004.subject: amino_acids
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000004.question: How many essential amino acids are there?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000004.answer_short: Wallach counts 12 the body can't make (mainstream says 9; he adds tyrosine, arginine, taurine, histidine). Miss any for long and a specific deficiency disease follows.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000057.subject: amino_acids
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000057.question: What does each amino acid do?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000057.answer_short: Many build protein (valine, lysine, leucine...); tryptophan makes niacin and serotonin; phenylalanine makes thyroid hormone and adrenaline; methionine makes choline and creatine.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000003.subject: macronutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000003.question: Are carbohydrates an essential nutrient?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000003.answer_short: No, says Wallach - the body can make all the carbs and sugar it needs by breaking down and rebuilding fats and proteins, so none has to come from the diet.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000051.subject: macronutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000051.question: What are carbohydrates?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000051.answer_short: The body's convenient fuel (but not essential) - plants build them from CO2 and water by photosynthesis. Sized as single sugars, double sugars, and long chains like starch and fiber.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000052.subject: macronutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000052.question: What are fats?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000052.answer_short: Water-repelling molecules packing ~9 calories a gram (vs 4.5); mostly triglycerides (glycerol + fatty acids). Fatty acids differ by chain length, saturation, and 'omega' number.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000055.subject: macronutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000055.question: What are proteins?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000055.answer_short: The body's most abundant carbon compound - the main stuff of muscle and every cell, and enzymes are proteins too. Built from amino acids linked by peptide bonds; they add nitrogen.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000056.subject: macronutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000056.question: Can you eat too much protein?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000056.answer_short: Wallach's view: a healthy person can eat even 300 g of protein a day (nearly 3/4 lb of meat) with no harm - as long as they have no kidney or liver disease and supplement properly.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000084.subject: light_therapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000084.question: What does ultraviolet (UV) light therapy treat?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000084.answer_short: Wallach says UV light boosts vitamin D and the immune system, and treats sore throats, vaginitis, ringworm, athlete's foot and eczema.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000085.subject: light_therapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000085.question: How is infrared light therapy done?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000085.answer_short: A local immune boost - shine infrared (a heat lamp) on a trigger point through a 1 cm hole until it reddens, drawing in white cells to help chronic wounds, bedsores and arthritis.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000086.subject: light_therapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000086.question: Is UV light therapy safe for the eyes?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000086.answer_short: Therapeutic UV is 'cool' (no heat) and helps skin diseases and arthritis while killing germs - but it can burn the eyes, so wear goggles or don't look at the lamp.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000087.subject: light_therapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000087.question: How does UV therapy actually work?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000087.answer_short: Its rays span 500-3,100 Angstroms, peaking at 2,537 - the wavelength that gives UV its germicidal, skin-reddening and vitamin-D-making power; visible light is only ~5% of the output.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000088.subject: chiropractic
WAL-CLM-LETS-000088.question: What is chiropractic?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000088.answer_short: A drug-free, surgery-free physical medicine holding that many ills come from 'subluxations' (misaligned vertebrae) pressing on spinal nerves - the West's most accepted alternative therapy.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000089.subject: chiropractic
WAL-CLM-LETS-000089.question: Where does chiropractic come from?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000089.answer_short: Spinal manipulation is ancient (Egypt, China, Babylon); it reached the West in 1895 when D.D. Palmer reportedly cured a janitor's deafness, and chiropractors won a 1987 antitrust case against the AMA.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000093.subject: aromatherapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000093.question: What is aromatherapy?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000093.answer_short: Massage with plant essential oils (from roots, flowers, leaves, bark, resin); Wallach says they act as pesticides, fungicides and hormone-like agents and help scars, acne and stretch marks.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000094.subject: aromatherapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000094.question: What are specific essential oils used for?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000094.answer_short: Wallach's list: Mexican yam for birth control, sarsaparilla for testosterone, peppermint for intestinal spasm, calamus to lower blood pressure, lemon as an expectorant, and hops/fennel for estrogens.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000095.subject: ayurveda
WAL-CLM-LETS-000095.question: What is Ayurveda, and how old is it?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000095.answer_short: Possibly the most ancient medical art - 'ayur' (life) + 'veda' (science), recorded ~1200 BC. 80-90% of Indians use it, and Wallach says the Greeks (even Pythagoras) learned medicine from the East Indians.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000096.subject: ayurveda
WAL-CLM-LETS-000096.question: How does Ayurveda explain health and disease?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000096.answer_short: The body is seven tissues (Dhatus) kept in balance by food, so 'wrong food' causes disease; it works with the energies Pitta, Kapha and Vaya and five elements, treating imbalances rather than diagnoses.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000112.subject: homeopathy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000112.question: What is homeopathy?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000112.answer_short: A system on two principles: 'like cures like' (a substance that causes symptoms in the healthy can cure a disease with those symptoms) and 'minimum dose' - using extremely diluted preparations.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000113.subject: homeopathy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000113.question: Who founded homeopathy, and does the dilution really work?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000113.answer_short: Samuel Hahnemann, who found Cinchona bark gave healthy people malaria-like symptoms; oddly, more dilute often meant a stronger effect - though past about 12C not one molecule of the original remains.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000106.subject: hydrotherapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000106.question: What is hydrotherapy?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000106.answer_short: Healing with water - practiced since Roman times across all medicine, from sitz baths for hemorrhoids to whirlpools for injuries and mineral baths for arthritis; insurance often covers it if prescribed.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000107.subject: hydrotherapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000107.question: What are the different kinds of hydrotherapy?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000107.answer_short: Cold baths cut swelling; hot baths ease soreness; mineral baths help arthritis; steam baths detox heavy metals; sitz baths for hemorrhoids; epsom for edema; water fasts and colonics for detox.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000108.subject: negative_ion_therapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000108.question: What is negative ion therapy?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000108.answer_short: Using negatively charged air particles to prevent and treat disease - abundant in forests and at the beach (300-1,000 per cubic meter) but low in AC'd rooms; too many POSITIVE ions bring anxiety and depression.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000109.subject: negative_ion_therapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000109.question: What does negative ion therapy do?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000109.answer_short: Six effects - it lowers heart rate/BP, deepens breathing, speeds respiratory cilia, boosts glands and steadies brain rhythm - and Wallach says it especially helps asthma, allergies and cystic fibrosis.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000110.subject: urine_therapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000110.question: What is urine therapy?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000110.answer_short: Injecting a patient's own urine back into them to boost immunity - the same idea as an allergist's shots; Wallach says MD allergists used it for 50 years until prepared allergens became profitable.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000111.subject: urine_therapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000111.question: How is urine therapy performed?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000111.answer_short: Urine is centrifuged and filtered to remove cells and bacteria, then 5-10 mL is injected under the skin (procaine stops any sting); Wallach cites use for allergies, asthma, migraine and arthritis.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000194.subject: urine_therapy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000194.question: How do autoimmune urine and blood therapies work?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000194.answer_short: They rev the body's defenses against foreign substances - including cancer proteins - much the way allergy shots build tolerance to pollen.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000083.subject: macrobiotics
WAL-CLM-LETS-000083.question: Why does the macrobiotic (brown-rice) diet work?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000083.answer_short: Wallach's take: its successes come mostly from accidentally cutting gluten - people with hidden celiac disease finally absorb minerals, vitamins and fats. The value is nutritional, not the yin/yang theory.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000115.subject: macrobiotics
WAL-CLM-LETS-000115.question: Where did macrobiotics come from?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000115.answer_short: George Ohsawa created it in 1946 Japan, using it to heal his own tuberculosis, then opened a healing center and toured the world teaching a philosophy of health through eating.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000116.subject: macrobiotics
WAL-CLM-LETS-000116.question: What is the macrobiotic diet?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000116.answer_short: An eating system built on balancing 'yin' (fruit, drinks, sweet) and 'yang' (meat, grains, dense) foods; reported to help food allergies, diabetes and - when wheat is dropped - grain sensitivity.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000104.subject: herbal_medicine
WAL-CLM-LETS-000104.question: What is herbal medicine?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000104.answer_short: An ancient system using plants to prevent and cure disease - the root of Chinese, Ayurvedic, American Indian and naturopathic medicine, traced back to Chinese pharmacopeias around 3000 BC.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000105.subject: herbal_medicine
WAL-CLM-LETS-000105.question: Do real drugs come from herbs?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000105.answer_short: Yes - Wallach notes over 30% of orthodox pharmaceuticals derive from plants (digitalis from foxglove, the cancer drug vincristine from periwinkle), and praises herbs' relative safety and millennia of use.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000475.subject: be_your_own_doctor
WAL-CLM-LETS-000475.question: What does Wallach mean by 'be your own doctor'?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000475.answer_short: Become your own primary care provider - you're unlikely to harm yourself. Try conservative and alternative care before orthodox medicine, and 'separate medicine and state.'

WAL-CLM-LETS-000476.subject: be_your_own_doctor
WAL-CLM-LETS-000476.question: What's the best health insurance?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000476.answer_short: Not getting sick. Prevention - a baseline supplement program and daily self-care - is cheaper and easier than illness; Wallach calls it the best buy for your health dollars.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000473.subject: be_your_own_doctor
WAL-CLM-LETS-000473.question: How should you choose a medical specialist?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000473.answer_short: Only when truly needed - then get three-plus opinions from different fields, ask to speak with ten past patients, and start conservative; the more 'exotic' the specialist, the higher the risk.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000474.subject: be_your_own_doctor
WAL-CLM-LETS-000474.question: How impaired are conventional doctors?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000474.answer_short: Wallach cites alarming numbers - tens of thousands of physician alcoholics, heavy drug use among doctors and students, and the U.S. losing 'seven medical-school classes' a year to addiction and suicide.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000481.subject: be_your_own_doctor
WAL-CLM-LETS-000481.question: How do you take charge of your home environment?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000481.answer_short: Grow some food and treat your home water and air - Wallach says 3,000+ mostly-carcinogenic chemicals slip through city water (clear isn't safe); a bone-charcoal filter removes them.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000362.subject: be_your_own_doctor
WAL-CLM-LETS-000362.question: What is 'metabolic therapy'?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000362.answer_short: Wallach's umbrella term for curing disease by fixing whole-body metabolism - through nutrition, herbs, homeopathy, acupuncture, manipulation and hydrotherapy.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000477.subject: hospital_dangers
WAL-CLM-LETS-000477.question: How dangerous are hospitals?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000477.answer_short: Wallach's tally: 970 of 1,000 hospitals billed wrong (always in their favor), up to half of new equipment defective on arrival, and 100,000+ deaths a year from hospital-caught infections.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000478.subject: hospital_dangers
WAL-CLM-LETS-000478.question: What should you do if you're hospitalized?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000478.answer_short: Have a family member stay to check every shot, pill and procedure before it's given, confirm your IV lines, and use family blood if needed - just as orthodox doctors monitor their own families.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000479.subject: hospital_dangers
WAL-CLM-LETS-000479.question: What is the 'medical industrial Bermuda Triangle'?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000479.answer_short: Wallach's name for the FDA, AMA and drug companies - costing Americans more than national defense while the U.S. ranks 17th in longevity and 32nd in birth defects. He calls to 'separate Medicine and State.'

WAL-CLM-LETS-000467.subject: pregnancy_birth
WAL-CLM-LETS-000467.question: Is a hospital birth necessary?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000467.answer_short: Wallach says pregnancy is normal, not a disease, and home birth is the safest, cheapest option - he delivered ~200 babies at home with one c-section, and blames the 35% hospital c-section rate on economics.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000468.subject: pregnancy_birth
WAL-CLM-LETS-000468.question: What prenatal care can a woman do herself?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000468.answer_short: A lot: self breast and pelvic exams, cycle tracking, home pregnancy tests, OTC prenatal vitamins, own blood-pressure and urine tests - and, barring a few specific risks, she can give birth at home.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000469.subject: pregnancy_birth
WAL-CLM-LETS-000469.question: What birth control can you buy without a prescription?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000469.answer_short: Condoms, spermicidal creams, jellies, foams and sponges - all over the counter. Wallach considers these barrier methods much safer than IUDs (the Dalkon Shield) and the pill (clots, deaths, sterility).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000470.subject: pregnancy_birth
WAL-CLM-LETS-000470.question: What causes most birth defects?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000470.answer_short: Wallach's 'pet peeve': 98% come from nutritional deficiencies, not radiation. Teens have more than women over 40 - and lab animals get defect-free diets, so why feed a rat better than a pregnant woman?

WAL-CLM-LETS-000472.subject: pregnancy_birth
WAL-CLM-LETS-000472.question: Is infertility a nutrition problem?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000472.answer_short: Wallach says mostly yes - as a breeder feeds a mare 120 days before mating, he's reversed hundreds of cases by nourishing both partners; one 'infertile' doctor had vitamin A at 10% of normal (malabsorption).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000480.subject: pregnancy_birth
WAL-CLM-LETS-000480.question: Which agency said women should supplement before pregnancy?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000480.answer_short: The CDC, in 1992 - not the FDA. Wallach credits the CDC's independence from company revenue, and notes it independently echoed his own preconception-supplementation thesis.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000471.subject: cystic_fibrosis
WAL-CLM-LETS-000471.question: Is cystic fibrosis really genetic?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000471.answer_short: Wallach's signature thesis: no - it's a selenium and essential-fatty-acid deficiency from the mother's malabsorption. He cites 1972 Cornell chicks cured in 21 days by selenium, and 450 patients treated since 1978.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000347.subject: longevity
WAL-CLM-LETS-000347.question: How long can humans live?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000347.answer_short: Wallach says 120-130 years, vs the ~72-78 of actuary tables. He credits the Hunza's ~100-year average to plant-derived colloidal minerals, and says filters, digestive aids and the baseline program add ~20 years.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000312.subject: vaccines
WAL-CLM-LETS-000312.question: What is Wallach's stance on vaccine mandates?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000312.answer_short: He calls immunization 'the greatest interface between government and freedom of choice,' opposes compulsory school mandates, defends the religious exemption, and says some experts blame certain vaccine programs for catastrophic diseases.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000232.subject: pregnancy_birth
WAL-CLM-LETS-000232.question: Why were midwives who knew contraception called witches?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000232.answer_short: Wallach notes midwives who knew contraception herbs were once branded 'witches' and burned; he ranks birth control (abstinence, barriers, hormones - least desirable, IUDs, surgery) and bluntly calls sex outside marriage 'Russian roulette.'

WAL-CLM-LETS-000263.subject: sexual_health
WAL-CLM-LETS-000263.question: How does Wallach approach premature ejaculation?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000263.answer_short: He calls it normal and curable, with physical causes (high expectation, infrequent sex, friction) not guilt; his fix is comfort with each other's bodies, frequent sex, and good lubrication, with ginseng and Zumbani as tonics.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000370.subject: home_remedies
WAL-CLM-LETS-000370.question: How can you repel mosquitoes naturally?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000370.answer_short: Screen doors and 'zapper' lights set 15-25 yards from the house draw mosquitoes off; Wallach adds pennyroyal oil on the skin and vitamin B1 at 500 mg/day as natural repellents - handy since mosquitoes carry malaria and encephalitis.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000090.subject: somatic_therapies
WAL-CLM-LETS-000090.question: What is osteopathy?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000090.answer_short: A manipulation-based healing art of body and spine, founded ~130 years ago by engineer Andrew Still after he lost all three children to orthodox medicine; today most D.O.s practice much like M.D.s.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000091.subject: somatic_therapies
WAL-CLM-LETS-000091.question: What is reflexology, and how is it meant to work?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000091.answer_short: An ancient Chinese and East Indian system: 'zones' on the soles and palms map to the internal organs, so 10-30 minutes of thumb compression on a point is meant to treat the organ it stands for.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000092.subject: somatic_therapies
WAL-CLM-LETS-000092.question: What is Rolfing (structural integration)?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000092.answer_short: A deep, uncomfortable connective-tissue massage devised by Ida Rolf to break down 'pathological' tissue and correct posture - said to leave patients half an inch to an inch taller.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000102.subject: faith_healing
WAL-CLM-LETS-000102.question: What is faith healing (laying-on-of-hands)?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000102.answer_short: Using a person to mediate healing through belief - recorded in ancient China and Egypt and in Christianity today. Wallach notes 20-60% of patients improve on placebo when positive thought is induced.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000103.subject: faith_healing
WAL-CLM-LETS-000103.question: Who are the Christian Scientists, and what is 'therapeutic touch'?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000103.answer_short: A Christian sect founded in 1879 by Mary Baker Eddy that holds 'healing is proof of God's love'; Wallach says they outlive other Westerners (and get lower insurance rates). Its modern nursing form is 'therapeutic touch.'

WAL-CLM-LETS-000114.subject: naturopathy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000114.question: What is naturopathy?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000114.answer_short: A whole system of natural medicine (N.D.) built on 'FIRST DO NO HARM' and the body's own healing power - covering herbs, hydrotherapy, homeopathy, nutrition and natural childbirth, but not major surgery or most drugs.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000097.subject: homeopathy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000097.question: What are Schuessler cell salts (Biochemics)?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000097.answer_short: A 19th-century system from Dr. Wilhelm Schuessler, who analyzed the ash of cremated bodies and found twelve mineral 'salts' he called essential to health; given in homeopathic (highly diluted) doses. Later workers added ~30 trace elements.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000098.subject: homeopathy
WAL-CLM-LETS-000098.question: What are Bach flower remedies?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000098.answer_short: Homeopathic-style flower preparations from bacteriologist Edward Bach (1880-1936), who first collected sun-warmed flower dew; aimed at emotional imbalance rather than physical disease, taken as four drops four times a day.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000117.subject: vitamins
WAL-CLM-LETS-000117.question: What is megavitamin (orthomolecular) therapy?
WAL-CLM-LETS-000117.answer_short: Using vitamins at very high 'pharmacologic' doses - the 1968 'megavitamin theory' that Linus Pauling named 'orthomolecular medicine' and Abram Hoffer extended to psychiatry, reportedly for colds, depression and schizophrenia, though orthodoxy never endorsed it.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000112.subject: rare_earth_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000112.question: What is dysprosium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000112.answer_short: A soft, silvery rare-earth metal -- the 9th most abundant of the rare earths -- discovered in 1886 and named from the Greek for 'hard to get at.' Its magnetic alloys help CDs work, and in the body it collects in bone.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000113.subject: rare_earth_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000113.question: What is erbium used for?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000113.answer_short: A scarce rare-earth metal (found 1843), alloyed with vanadium to improve workability; its most memorable use is tinting glass and enamel pink -- the pink glass of sunglasses and costume jewelry. In the body it settles in bone.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000114.subject: rare_earth_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000114.question: What is europium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000114.answer_short: One of the rarest rare earths, isolated in 1901 and named for Europe; it is the softest of them and so reactive it bursts into flame in air above 150C. It is mined from the ores monazite and bastnasite.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000137.subject: rare_earth_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000137.question: Where is gadolinium found?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000137.answer_short: A rare-earth mineral scattered through rocks and plants -- hickory trees can concentrate it to 70 ppm -- and in land animals it collects in the bone and liver almost as soon as it is absorbed.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000172.subject: rare_earth_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000172.question: What is holmium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000172.answer_short: A soft, silvery rare-earth metal the body carries in trace amounts, mostly in bone. Spotted by its spectral 'fingerprint' in 1878 as unknown 'element X,' it was isolated in 1879 and named Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000203.subject: rare_earth_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000203.question: What is lutetium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000203.answer_short: The last lanthanide -- the hardest, heaviest and one of the least abundant rare earths, silvery-white and corrosion-resistant. Discovered independently in 1907 and named for Lutetia, the ancient name of Paris.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000112.subject: rare_earth_elements
WAL-CLM-RARE-000112.question: Does cerium have a medical use?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000112.answer_short: Yes -- cerium (a rare earth that accumulates in bone) is used as cerium nitrate, a topical disinfectant for severe burn victims.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000035.subject: obscure_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000035.question: What is actinium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000035.answer_short: A naturally radioactive metal that glows in the dark like radium (its name is Greek for 'ray'). Wallach lists it among elements found in living tissue -- it gathers in bone and liver, where he speculates it may have a metabolic role, though he assigns it no health use.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000048.subject: obscure_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000048.question: Where does the word 'bromide' come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000048.answer_short: From medicine: sodium bromide, a bromine salt, was a common mild sedative in the late 1800s prescribed to calm the nerves -- which is why we still speak of taking a 'bromide' to settle down.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000095.subject: obscure_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000095.question: How was cesium discovered?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000095.answer_short: In 1860 the German chemists Bunsen and Kirchhoff identified cesium by its spectral 'fingerprint' -- the colors of light it emits when heated. Its lines were sky-blue, so they named it from the Latin caesius, 'sky blue.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000158.subject: obscure_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000158.question: Why was hafnium discovered so late?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000158.answer_short: Because it hid inside its chemical 'twin' zirconium -- common in the crust but nearly impossible to separate, so it was not isolated until 1923. Coster and de Hevesy named it Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor Niels Bohr's home city.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000185.subject: obscure_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000185.question: What is indium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000185.answer_short: A rare, soft, bluish-white metal that resists corrosion and 'shrieks' when bent; it is a byproduct of refining zinc. Discovered in 1863 by its bright violet spectral line, it is named from the Latin indicum, 'indigo.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000186.subject: obscure_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000186.question: What is iridium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000186.answer_short: One of the hardest, most corrosion-resistant metals known -- a precious metal like platinum. Smithson Tennant isolated it in 1803 from platinum-ore residues and named it for the Latin iris ('rainbow'), after its vividly colored salts.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000085.subject: cobalt
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000085.question: What does cobalt have to do with vitamin B12?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000085.answer_short: Cobalt is the heart of vitamin B12 -- it sits in a ring related to the ones holding iron in hemoglobin and magnesium in chlorophyll, and gives B12 its red color. 'Cyanocobalamine' was named for a cyanide group on the first B12 isolated (1948).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000086.subject: cobalt
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000086.question: How do animals get vitamin B12 from cobalt?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000086.answer_short: Microbes do the work: gut bacteria in a cow's rumen turn elemental cobalt into B12, which the animal absorbs. Carnivores get it secondhand from prey, and rabbits and rodents eat their own night feces (coprophagy) to recover it.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000156.subject: helium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000156.question: What is helium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000156.answer_short: The lightest noble gas -- so inert it forms no compounds and occurs pure in nature. After hydrogen it is the 2nd most abundant element in the universe (~7% of atoms). It was the first element found off Earth: seen in the sun's spectrum in 1868 and named from Greek Helios, 'sun.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000157.subject: helium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000157.question: Why do deep-sea divers breathe helium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000157.answer_short: Because helium dissolves in blood far less than nitrogen, so less gas builds up under pressure and the risk of 'the bends' drops. The bends hits when a diver surfaces too fast and dissolved gas fizzes out of the blood into the joints -- like a just-opened soda.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000031.subject: silver
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000031.question: What was colloidal silver used for?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000031.answer_short: Wallach relays older medical reports (not his own protocol): in 1917-18 colloidal silver was described as soothing inflammation and helping prostate/bladder irritation, itching, catarrh, even a post-childbirth blood infection. Silver sulfadiazine is still used in ~70% of U.S. burn centers.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000077.subject: cadmium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000077.question: Why is cadmium toxic?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000077.answer_short: It is a non-essential heavy metal that piles up in the kidneys, and tobacco concentrates it -- so smokers and bystanders breathe it in. The danger is that cadmium mimics zinc and can shove it out of zinc-dependent enzymes.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000046.subject: bismuth
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000046.question: What is bismuth used for, and did stress really cause ulcers?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000046.answer_short: Bismuth is the pink in Pepto-Bismol, used for stomach ulcers and gut infections for millennia. Wallach's myth-buster: ulcers were blamed on stress for decades, but the real cause is Helicobacter pylori bacteria (Marshall & Warren, 1983) -- treated with antibiotics, antacids and bismuth.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000050.subject: carbon
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000050.question: What is Wallach's view on global warming?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000050.answer_short: Off nutrition, he is skeptical of blaming humans -- calling our share of Earth's biomass 'pitifully small' and noting Ice Ages and warm spells have always cycled naturally. His fix is simply to plant more trees, which pull carbon dioxide from the air. (His personal stance on a debated topic.)

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000147.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000147.question: What is hydrogen?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000147.answer_short: The simplest atom -- one proton, one electron -- and the most abundant element in the universe (~93% of all atoms). As a gas it is diatomic (H2), colorless and highly flammable, burning with oxygen to make water; its name is Greek for 'water-maker.'

WAL-CLM-RARE-000276.subject: drug_safety_elderly
WAL-CLM-RARE-000276.question: Which tranquilizers and sleeping pills are risky for older adults?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000276.answer_short: Wallach flags Valium (diazepam), Librium (chlordiazepoxide) and Dalmane (flurazepam) as too long-acting or addictive -- they cause drowsiness, confusion and falls in the elderly. His fix: address the underlying need with minerals (calcium, magnesium, lithium, chromium, vanadium) and cut sugar and caffeine.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000277.subject: drug_safety_elderly
WAL-CLM-RARE-000277.question: What other tranquilizers and sleeping pills should older adults avoid?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000277.answer_short: The second half of Wallach's list: Miltown (meprobamate), Nembutal (pentobarbital) and Seconal (secobarbital) -- all addictive, long-acting and fall-prone. Same mineral replacement: calcium, magnesium, lithium, chromium and vanadium.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000284.subject: drug_safety_elderly
WAL-CLM-RARE-000284.question: Which muscle relaxants are risky for older adults?
WAL-CLM-RARE-000284.answer_short: Wallach flags Flexeril (cyclobenzaprine), Norflex (orphenadrine), Robaxin (methocarbamol) and Soma (carisoprodol) -- they cause dizziness, drowsiness, fainting and falls. His mineral replacement: calcium, magnesium, boron and lithium.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000019.subject: homosexuality
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000019.question: Does Wallach think homosexuality is a lifestyle choice?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000019.answer_short: No. Wallach reframes it as a prenatal, congenital event -- a preventable deficiency of minerals or vitamins in early pregnancy, not a learned behavior or a choice.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000008.subject: homosexuality
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000008.question: What does Wallach say happens in the brain to cause homosexuality?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000008.answer_short: He points to underdevelopment of the preoptic hypothalamus, so the brain's sense of gender diverges from the genetic gender carried in the chromosomes.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000022.subject: homosexuality
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000022.question: What brain-anatomy research does Wallach cite on homosexuality?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000022.answer_short: He cites Simon LeVay's autopsy studies finding the preoptic hypothalamus smaller in homosexual men, plus differences in the anterior commissure and a prenatal testosterone surge.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000023.subject: homosexuality
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000023.question: Is there a 'gay gene'?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000023.answer_short: Wallach says no -- identical twins are only about 50% concordant, so he argues it is congenital but not genetic; he quotes geneticist Dean Hamer that there is no gay gene.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000024.subject: homosexuality
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000024.question: Why does Wallach think homosexuality has become more common?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000024.answer_short: He ties the rise in reported homosexuality to the steady decline of minerals in farm soils and the food supply, citing Kinsey and later prevalence figures.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000026.subject: homosexuality
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000026.question: Does Wallach think homosexuality can be prevented?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000026.answer_short: He says a complete preconception nutrition program -- the 90 essential nutrients -- could prevent it; from his interviews he holds it is congenital, so it cannot be prayed away or coached away.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000020.subject: intersex
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000020.question: What does 'intersex' mean?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000020.answer_short: Intersex is the modern medical term for what was once called hermaphroditism -- a range of congenital variations in sexual anatomy; one 1969 catalogue listed 98 distinct types.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000009.subject: intersex
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000009.question: What causes intersex conditions, and can they be prevented?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000009.answer_short: Wallach ties them to mineral or vitamin deficiency in the embryo -- citing John Money's estimate of up to 4% of births -- and argues they could be avoided with complete preconception nutrition.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000025.subject: intersex
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000025.question: What do animals reveal about intersex birth defects?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000025.answer_short: Every human congenital sexual defect also appears in animals from embryonic malnutrition -- like the 'freemartin,' a masculinized female calf twinned with a male; scarcer nutrition means more defects.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000021.subject: intersex
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000021.question: How have intersex and homosexual people been regarded through history?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000021.answer_short: Wallach traces it from Plato's 'three sexes' and the Hermes-plus-Aphrodite root of 'hermaphrodite' through executions of intersex people to modern cases like Christine Jorgenson and Olympic sex testing.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000017.subject: pregnancy_birth
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000017.question: How were birth defects explained before modern medicine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000017.answer_short: Wallach surveys centuries of theories -- Renaissance omens and divine punishment, early teratology collections -- up to the 1961 thalidomide disaster that proved drugs can deform a fetus.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000018.subject: pregnancy_birth
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000018.question: What does Wallach say is the most common cause of birth defects?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000018.answer_short: Deficiency of one or more of the 90 essential nutrients in the mother before conception and through the first 90 days of pregnancy -- proven, he says, by an animal industry that breeds out birth defects with nutrition.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000027.subject: quackbusters
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000027.question: What are the 'Quackbusters' and what does Wallach say about them?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000027.answer_short: Wallach calls the Quackbusters a group of doctors organized to destroy alternative-medicine competition, and rejects their claim that a varied diet alone supplies all the vitamins and minerals you need.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000028.subject: longevity
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000028.question: What did a Harvard survey find about where Americans live longest?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000028.answer_short: A 1990 survey found the longest-living Americans were Scandinavian-heritage dairy farmers who poached, stewed and baked their food, while the shortest-lived regions fried everything -- diet, not doctors, drove the gap.
